summary: Furrow helps farmers choose what to plant, using 25 years of NASA data for their exact field. A farmer finds their field on a satellite map, draws its shape and enters what they grow now, their priorities and their limits (budget, machinery, crops they can't sell, in any language). Furrow replays every crop rotation of one to six years, with every cover crop pattern (about 54 million combinations), day by day through 25 years of NASA POWER weather. It scores each one on profit, water, soil health, erosion and steady harvests in bad years, and ranks them by the farmer's own priorities. The result is a plain-language plan with numbers a farmer can check: days of bare soil, rain hitting unprotected ground, water missed in hot dry years, and income and risk in euros. As droughts become more frequent, choosing crops by habit gets riskier. Furrow turns NASA's view from space into a decision on the ground, free, in any browser.
details:
Furrow is a free web app that finds the best crop rotation for one specific field. The farmer marks the field on the map, says what they grow now, how much each goal matters to them (now and in the long run), and what they can realistically take on: an acceptable drop in income, a machinery budget, cover crop seed, crops they cannot grow or sell, or any limit written in their own words.

How does it work, though?

Shows weather for 25 years (2001 to 2025) of daily NASA POWER data for the field: temperature, rain, sun, wind, humidity and root-zone soil wetness.

Has slopes from elevation data for every square of the drawn shape, soil texture from SoilGrids, and how the field actually grows from MODIS and Sentinel-2 greenness.

Sowing and harvest dates are worked out from the field's own frost dates and warmth, and checked against USDA usual dates and against what the satellite saw.

For each rotation and each of the 25 years, rain fills the soil, the crop draws water and the extra drains away.

Every rotation of 1 to 6 years with every cover crop pattern (53,979,471 in our example field) is scored on five goals: profit after costs, saving water, building soil health, keeping soil in place, and steady harvests in bad years. The scores are weighted by the farmer's priorities, with a separate plan for the first years and for the long run.

Each rotation gets a margin per hectare (yield x price minus seed, fertiliser, spraying, drying, fuel and cover crop costs, with nitrogen savings after legumes), replayed 3,000 times with weather, crop prices and gas-driven fertiliser costs moving together. This gives a bad, typical and good year and the chance of a loss.

The years are reshuffled, and the weather is made warmer and drier to check the answer is not luck.

What does the farmer get?

A clear plan, the evidence behind it (for example, bare soil cut from 157 to 25 days a year), a calendar showing when heavy rain falls on bare ground, how each rotation copes with hot dry, typical and cool wet years, live NASA map layers (MODIS greenness, SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall), and a full PDF report to take to an adviser.

Droughts are becoming more frequent across Europe and the Black Sea region. Most farmers choose crops by habit and get advice made for a whole region. Furrow gives them a field-specific, evidence-based plan for free, with no sensors, subscription or installation. It works for any field NASA data covers.

Why is it creative?

Instead of predicting one season, Furrow tests every possible rotation against every past season, and shows the result in the farmer's terms: euros, days of bare soil and bad years. It is honest about its limits: weather is a 50 km grid, prices are typical values, and it is not yet reviewed by an agronomist.

Tools used:

JavaScript (no framework), HTML and CSS; Leaflet for maps; a Cloudflare Worker as a data proxy; Cloudflare Workers AI (open Llama and Mistral models) to read limits written in any language; GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/kuzakaa/furrow
